articles.content_orig:
Apple has announced that the long-running Apple Support Community discussion forums for user-to-user tech support will be permanently closing on Friday, November 20. The forums have existed in some form for nearly 30 years, so it is the end of an era.
Effective immediately, the Apple Support Community forums are in a read-only state, with new posts no longer being accepted. The final message posted to the site appears to have been submitted at 5:49 p.m. Pacific Time on November 10.
Apple's notice to visitors:
The Apple Support Community will permanently close on November 20, 2026. Starting today, the site will no longer accept new posts and is available in a read-only state.
You can continue to find trusted guidance and support on the official Apple Support site .
We want to thank the community members who have contributed their time and expertise to help others with their Apple products.
The forums have a 28-year history. Apple offered an online discussion forum for user-to-user tech support since 1998, when it launched the Apple Tech Exchange. The forums were renamed to Apple Discussions in 2000, and then to the Apple Support Communities in 2011, before taking on their current Apple Support Community name in 2022.
Apple informed MacRumors that it decided to sunset the Apple Support Community after a careful evaluation of strategy and customer needs.
Alternatives to the Apple Support Community include the MacRumors Forums and Reddit , and customers can continue to contact Apple Support .

articles.title_orig: Russian casualties ‘reach 450,000’: What that means for the Ukraine war
articles.title_zh: Russian casualties ‘reach 450,000’: What that means for the Ukraine war
articles.content_orig:
Records leaked from Rosstat, Russia’s state statistics agency, have shown that at least 450,000 Russians, most of them soldiers, died in the war in Ukraine up to August this year.
Among the dead were more than 4,000 foreign citizens who are believed to have died fighting for Russia, from countries including Uzbekistan, Tajikistan, Nepal, Colombia and Nigeria.
The records were obtained by two hacking groups, the Belarusian Cyber Partisans and Ukraine’s Silent Crow.
Rosstat confirmed it had been hit by cyberattacks between October 29 and November 1, but said it found no evidence that its databases had been compromised or that protected data leaked.
Moscow does not officially publish its military death toll.
Deaths can take months, and sometimes years, to be registered, in Russia. Investigations for The Financial Times (FT) have concluded that once late paperwork is counted, the toll up to August will settle at about 550,000.
So what do the leaked records show, and what do they tell us about who is fighting Russia’s war? Here’s what you need to know:
The Cyber Partisans and Silent Crow said on November 1 that they had broken into Rosstat’s network.
The two hacking groups published their own analysis of the records and shared the files with several news organisations, though the data has not been independently verified.
However, media outlets and analysts say they believe it is real.
Janis Kluge, an expert on Russia at the German Institute for International and Security Affairs, wrote on X: “There is no longer any doubt that the leaked Rosstat database is authentic. You can find any famous person who has died in recent years.”
However, in a later post he added: “The trickier question is: Was the data manipulated to increase the war death toll?” before adding, “This would [be] unbelievably difficult, so this is a highly unlikely conspiracy theory”.
A death toll far beyond anything Moscow has admitted so far.
The files list about 410,000 deaths directly as war-related, and 42,000 more fighting-age men whose deaths were confirmed in court because their bodies have never been recovered.
The FT identified another 12,000 likely military deaths among men who died at or near the front, bringing the total to at least 450,000.
About 120,000 of those with a recorded location died in the area containing Avdiivka and Pokrovsk, and a further 48,000 in Bakhmut, the FT reported.
Avdiivka is a small industrial city in the Donetsk region. After Russian-backed forces seized parts of eastern Ukraine in 2014 and 2015, it became part of the so-called “contact line”, and Ukrainian forces spent years fortifying the city.
When Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022, it was the subject of two years of bitter fighting before Russia took it in 2024.
After the fall of Avdiivka, Russian forces moved towards the coal-mining city of Pokrovsk in the Donetsk region, capturing it in early 2026 after more than a year of gruelling battles that had left the city in ruins.
Bakhmut, a city in the Donetsk Oblast and situated at a vital intersection connecting eastern Ukraine with the rest of the country, was the site of the longest and bloodiest infantry battle of the war before falling to Russian and paramilitary Wagner Group forces in May 2023.
Older men from poorer, often minority regions.
The average age of those killed rose from 34 in the first year of the war to 40 in 2025, and men aged 35 to 44 made up the largest group, with 158,000 dead, the FT reported.
Ethnic Russians constitute more than two-thirds of Russia’s population of 143 million. The rest are minorities – from millions of ethnic Ukrainians and Tatars to smaller Indigenous groups in Siberia and the Arctic.
Zabaykalsky Krai, home to a large community of Buryats, an Indigenous Mongolic people of southern Siberia, recorded about 12,300 deaths, roughly one for every 80 people in the region, the FT reported.
Bashkortostan, another region with a large minority population including Indigenous Bashkirs and Volga Tatars, recorded 15,800 deaths.
More than 4,000, and possibly far more.
The FT identified 4,141 probable foreign soldiers holding foreign citizenship among the dead.
Bloomberg News, using a wider definition that includes people born outside Russia, counted 11,335, with foreign deaths rising from about 630 in 2022 to more than 5,500 in 2025.
Deaths of Nepalis were concentrated in 2023 and 2024, and those of Colombians, Kenyans and Nigerians from late 2025, Bloomberg reported.
The FT counted the highest death toll from Uzbekistan at 807, followed by Tajikistan with 598. There were also 44 Nepali dead and 98 Colombians, the highest toll from Latin America.
About 340 Africans are among the dead, most of them killed since 2025, Bloomberg reported.
Nigeria, Cameroon and Egypt had the highest tolls, with 127 deaths between them, according to the FT.
Furthermore, Ukrainian officials believe Russia deployed some 14,000 North Korean troops to hold off Ukraine’s 2024 incursion into the Kursk region, but they do not appear in the leaked data.
Mostly for the money, and often after being misled.
An estimated 28,000 foreigners from 136 countries are said to be fighting in the Russian army overall.
An Amnesty International report in September found that people from Brazil, Colombia, Sri Lanka and South Africa had been promised well-paid civilian jobs and then forced into the army on arrival in Russia.
The rights group spoke with foreign nationals currently serving with Russian forces and members of their families as well as lawyers, human rights activists and journalists.
It found local agents and misleading online job advertisements were being used to deceive foreign nationals in their home countries.
Nationals from 36 African countries are known to be fighting for Russia in the four-year war, Ukraine’s foreign minister said in November last year.
One South African man who applied online for a driving job in Poland was told to fly to Moscow, pick up a truck, and drive it to Poland.
His wife told Amnesty International: “Upon arrival to Moscow, everything was taken from him. He was told that he would not be going to Poland and that he is becoming a soldier.”
Many recruits were promised lucrative salaries and sign-up bonuses that were not then fulfilled, Amnesty reported.
In Kenya , where intelligence officials say more than 1,000 citizens have been recruited, agencies promised monthly wages of about $2,715 and bonuses of up to $9,309.
Moscow denies coercing anyone to fight in Ukraine.
They indicate that Russia is struggling for manpower.
The Institute for the Study of War, a Washington-based think tank, posted an analysis of the leaked data, saying the figures likely understate Russia’s true losses because of reporting limitations.
It added that, as of July, Russia’s casualties are now outpacing its recruitment.
Kluge told The Moscow Times that the deaths also represent about half a per cent of Russia’s working-age population, which may have little economic impact, so the main significance is political.
He added, “You cannot say Russia is winning this war if it is losing population at this rate.”

articles.title_orig: Italy says it backs Germany joining next-generation fighter jet project
articles.title_zh: Italy says it backs Germany joining next-generation fighter jet project
articles.content_orig:
France and Germany launched their flagship FCAS fighter project with too much ideology and too little attention to contractual details, German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius said on November 9, 2026, blaming industrial disagreements for its collapse.
Speaking alongside French Armed Forces Minister Catherine Vautrin at a hearing of the Franco-German Parliamentary Assembly in Berlin, Pistorius argued that the project had been launched before Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine with an overly large “ideological superstructure,” while insufficient attention was paid to its organizational structure and contractual arrangements.
According to a summary published by the Bundestag’s parliamentary news service , Pistorius said he regretted the end of FCAS but insisted that the governments were not responsible for its collapse. Instead, he blamed the industrial partners’ inability to reach an agreement, which he attributed in part to “how the contracts were set up at the time.”
“We must not repeat this mistake,” he warned.
The remarks follow years of disagreements between Dassault Aviation, the designated lead contractor for the New Generation Fighter (NGF), and Airbus, which represented German and Spanish industry.
When Airbus and Dassault announced their initial industrial agreement in June 2019 , they emphasized clear governance, joint decision-making and fair treatment of intellectual property rights. Dassault would lead fighter development, while Airbus would oversee the remote carriers and combat cloud. A first demonstrator flight was initially expected by 2026.
Those arrangements became increasingly contentious as the program progressed, particularly after Spain’s industrial entry in December 2020 gave Airbus a role on behalf of two of the three partner nations. Dassault CEO Éric Trappier insisted his company needed effective control over fighter development, while Airbus and German industry opposed arrangements that would reduce their decision-making authority.
The partners also faced diverging operational requirements. France needed a carrier-capable, nuclear-capable fighter , while Germany had no equivalent requirements.
Pistorius’s decision to absolve the governments is not universally shared. In a July 2026 policy brief for the German Council on Foreign Relations (DGAP), Emil Archambault argued that insufficient political direction had allowed disagreements over technical requirements, governance and industrial responsibilities to persist for years.
Despite repeated attempts at political mediation , Germany ended its participation in the joint NGF project in June 2026 .
Pistorius confirmed that the Global Combat Air Programme (GCAP), led by the UK, Italy and Japan, remained an option for Germany. However, he warned that the three partners had spent years negotiating their agreements, and admitting Germany would require their consent and potentially lengthy contractual adjustments.
Berlin is also considering a separate European fighter project led by Airbus. In June 2026, the company launched its Team Gen 6 initiative with seven other German aerospace and defense companies, including Hensoldt, MTU Aero Engines and Diehl Defence.
In an interview with the Funke Media Group published on November 7, 2026, Pistorius said Germany was examining both options and targeting a decision in the first quarter of 2027, with the Airbus-led option aiming for an operational fighter in the early 2040s.
London has signaled interest. British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on October 8, 2026, that the UK was open to Germany joining GCAP , with Airbus preparing for talks with BAE Systems over a possible role in the program.
Japan, however, has been more cautious. During Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s visit to Tokyo on October 28, 2026, Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi avoided mentioning GCAP at their joint press conference, despite Merz raising the possibility of German participation.
According to Jiji Press , Japanese officials fear that admitting Germany could delay development and jeopardize the planned 2035 entry into service, when Japan intends to begin replacing its F-2 fighters.
Japanese Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi addressed the issue on November 2, 2026, stressing that any additional partner would have to be considered in light of the development schedule and its impact on the defense industry.
For Germany, joining GCAP could therefore revive some of the same industrial and contractual disputes that brought down FCAS, this time within a program whose founding partners have already negotiated their respective responsibilities .
Vautrin offered a different assessment of FCAS, declining to describe it as a failure. She argued that work already completed would allow the partners to continue cooperating on networked combat capabilities, particularly the combat cloud intended to connect aircraft, drones and other military platforms.
On July 17, 2026, President Emmanuel Macron confirmed that the common aircraft and engine projects had stopped, while cooperation on other systems would continue. France has since moved ahead with national fighter development. Its draft 2027 defense budget outlines a second NGF demonstration phase beginning in 2027 , followed by full-scale development in 2029. Dassault CEO Éric Trappier has indicated that a demonstrator could fly in 2031 or 2032.
Whether the wider FCAS architecture can survive the loss of its common fighter remains unclear, particularly as France and Germany pursue separate aircraft with potentially different systems and operational requirements.
Beyond FCAS, Vautrin argued that European defense procurement should prioritize domestic industrial capabilities, warning that spending EU funds outside Europe would deepen existing dependencies.
Despite the fighter program’s collapse, France and Germany are also pursuing closer cooperation on nuclear deterrence . Vautrin recalled Paris’s offer to involve European partners in President Macron’s forward deterrence initiative unveiled in March 2026 .
Pistorius welcomed the offer but stressed that the United States remained Europe’s principal nuclear ally, while control over French nuclear weapons would remain exclusively in French hands.

articles.title_orig: Body found on French beach after attempted Channel crossing
articles.title_zh: Body found on French beach after attempted Channel crossing
articles.content_orig:
A man in his 20s has died following an attempted small boat crossing of the English channel, the French coastguard has reported.
Authorities said his body was found on Sainte-Cecile beach, near the coastal town of Le Touquet, on Saturday morning.
Overnight, a rescue team from France's Regional Operational Center for Surveillance (CROSS) had been deployed to monitor the boarding migrants onto a "makeshift vessel" at the beach, it said.
It reported that the vessel was stopped from departing by French authorities, and that no one was found in the water following a "thorough sweep".
The coastguard described the boarding process of the makeshift vessel as "chaotic", adding that five men were attended to by firefighters at the scene for signs of hypothermia.
A small craft was then deployed which - along with "land-based units" from the local fire and rescue service - conducted "a thorough sweep of the area but found no one in the water".
"Following the operation, at approximately 08:00 (09:00 GMT) the body of a man in his twenties was discovered on the beach," the coastguard reported.
It adds an investigation will be opened to "determine the circumstances surrounding the incident".
In the latest week of data, ending 8 November, the UK government reported that 903 migrants arrived by small boat into the UK in 14 boats.
A further 624 migrants were prevented from making the crossing, the data shows.
Earlier this year, Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood ordered an urgent review after two boats carrying 21 people landed in Kent without being intercepted .
"Our improved monitoring has led to uncontrolled crossings becoming incredibly rare, but even one is one too many," she said at the time.

articles.title_orig: MAGA turns on Lutnick amid China spy scandal
articles.title_zh: MAGA turns on Lutnick amid China spy scandal
articles.content_orig:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Friday accused the Commerce Department of a delay in labeling Nvidia customer Megaspeed a possible national security threat, publicly airing an ongoing administration blame game following the ouster of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.
His comments come as some of President Donald Trump’s advisers, reeling from the fallout of Huang’s resignation, have begun discussing whether Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick should be dismissed, according to people familiar with the conversations. Trump himself has also fielded calls from administration officials and outside advisors raising alarm bells about Lutnick, two additional people said.
So far, the White House has stood by him, issuing a statement Thursday – before Bessent’s comments – saying Trump “maintains complete confidence in the secretary and his ability to carry out the position as the most transformative Commerce Secretary in modern history.” Trump and Lutnick are longtime friends, and sources said it was unclear what the president might do.
Speaking on CNBC, Bessent said a wide swath of Trump’s administration — including the Treasury and State departments, the Pentagon and the US Trade Representative — favored placing Megaspeed on an export blacklist.
He said it was the Commerce Department, led by Lutnick, that had failed the follow through.
“Commerce…has the pen. You would have to ask them about their internal processes,” he said.
He suggested the inaction had violated directives given by Trump.
“I am frustrated when President Trump made it very clear that China should not receive any Nvidia chips above” a certain technological level, he said.
“And so any leakage is very frustrating because it hurts our great companies in the AI race, gives the Chinese an advantage,” he went on.
CNN has reached out to the Commerce Department for comment.
Trump officials have long harbored concerns that Megaspeed has circumvented US law and funneled advanced chips into China — a prospect that Treasury staffers argued should land it on Commerce’s so-called entity list of China-connected companies that could pose national security risks.
But the issue gathered newfound attention and importance in recent days when it was reported publicly that Huang had an affair with a Megaspeed employee suspected of having intelligence connections to China.
Senior Trump officials, including Lutnick, were briefed months ago about Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang, the Megaspeed executive.
Despite those warnings, Commerce has so far refused to put Megaspeed on the entity list, people familiar with the matter said.
In a tense Situation Room meeting last week, Bessent challenged Lutnick over his department’s reluctance to blacklist Megaspeed, CNN previously reported. Lutnick did not immediately commit to taking any specific action, they said.
In the interview Friday, Bessent did not deny the confrontation .
“We don’t repeat conversations in the Situation Room,” he said.

articles.title_orig: ISRAEL/PALESTINE: Statement by the High Representative on behalf of the European Union on the humanitarian developments in Gaza
articles.title_zh: ISRAEL/PALESTINE: Statement by the High Representative on behalf of the European Union on the humanitarian developments in Gaza
articles.content_orig:
The European Union has urged Israel to reopen all Gaza border crossings and grant “immediate, unimpeded access” for aid groups to provide humanitarian relief in the territory following devastating flooding in Gaza this week.
Civilian infrastructure and medical facilities in Gaza “must be protected,” said an EU statement released on Saturday by the office of Kaja Kallas, the EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs and the Vice-President of the European Commission.
The EU call came as an Israeli drone attack killed two more Palestinians in Gaza on Saturday.
The drone struck them as they walked down a street in Jabaliya on the northern edge of Gaza City, according to Mohamed Abu Selmiya, director of Shifa Hospital in Gaza City, where the casualties were taken. The American field hospital said several other people were wounded but did not provide a number.
The Israeli military said it struck two Hamas “militants” in the area.
An Israeli air attack on Thursday at the Nasser Medical Complex in southern Gaza killed at least six Palestinians, including a surgeon, and left dozens wounded.
“The EU underlines the need to respect international law, including international humanitarian law, at all times,” the 27-nation bloc said on Saturday. “This includes the protection of civilians and civilian infrastructure, as well as medical personnel and facilities. The recent airstrike on the Nasser Hospital is deeply alarming,” it added.
Damage from Israeli attacks on Gaza’s infrastructure has worsened floods caused by heavy rain, which have submerged large areas of the enclave, local officials and the UN said this week. Gaza’s media office reported that more than 700km of Gaza’s sewage network has been destroyed.
Heavy rain has directly affected at least 106,000 people in Gaza in recent days, according to the UN children’s agency, UNICEF, with thousands of tents for displaced Palestinians submerged and latrines overflowing into camps.
In response, the EU said that “Israel must enable the work of the UN and its agencies, and humanitarian organisations including NGOs, and comply with all its obligations under international law, including international humanitarian law and international human rights law.”
The EU reaffirmed “its commitment to the two-state solution” and called for “the full withdrawal of Israeli forces from Gaza” as it called for “sustained distribution of humanitarian assistance and early recovery support at scale” to ease the worsening humanitarian crisis in Gaza.

articles.title_orig: Eric Trump-backed robot soldier startup can't pay staff after founder borrowed $4.6 million from company to buy home
articles.title_zh: Eric Trump-backed robot soldier startup can't pay staff after founder borrowed $4.6 million from company to buy home
articles.content_orig:
Foundation Future Industries , a maker of military humanoid robots advised and backed by Eric Trump, failed to pay employees last month as its cash reserves dwindled, according to people with direct knowledge of the matter.
Workers have yet to receive paychecks after San Francisco-based Foundation missed payroll on Oct. 30, said the people, who asked for anonymity to speak candidly about a private company.
The situation has particularly angered some inside the startup because its CEO and co-founder, Sankaet Pathak , borrowed $4.6 million from the company last year to buy a luxury home, money that could have been used to pay workers, the people said.
Public records show that an LLC that names Pathak as sole principal purchased a $4.6 million Sausalito, California, property with "sweeping, cinematic views" of the San Francisco Bay in October 2025.
A spokesman for Pathak acknowledged receiving a detailed list of the major points from this story on Thursday, but didn't respond to requests for comment. Pathak's previous startup, a fintech firm named Synapse, collapsed in 2024, leaving thousands of Americans locked out of their savings accounts .
Foundation's cash crunch comes at a precarious moment for the company, which Pathak has said is close to unveiling a next-generation, weapons-ready robot that will help the U.S. compete against Chinese rivals. At the same time, Pathak is seeking to raise hundreds of millions of dollars in funding at a $3 billion valuation.
The company has garnered headlines this year for Pathak's claims that his robots could soon take on battlefield tasks in Ukraine or patrol the U.S. border with Mexico. Broadcast interviews and articles about Foundation also include claims that the company has won $24 million in Pentagon contracts.
"What we're about to unveil in the next couple of months [is] going to be the strongest humanoid robot that exists anywhere in the world, including China," Pathak said in an April television interview.
That April interview introduced Eric Trump, the son of the U.S. president, as a Foundation investor and chief strategy advisor. It is unclear how large his stake is.
Eric Trump and his brother Donald Trump Jr. have invested in an array of defense firms, including makers of military drones and autonomous weapons. A July Washington Post investigation found that startups backed by investment vehicles linked to the brothers had secured at least $3.2 billion in government business.
"We have to win robotics in the United States of America," Eric Trump said in April. "When you go up and interact with these robots ... they fist bump you, they high five you, they follow your commands."
Eric Trump's involvement in Foundation drew the swift ire of Sen. Elizabeth Warren , D-Mass., who asked whether Foundation won U.S. defense contracts because of nepotism.
"Eric Trump went on FOX to brag about winning ANOTHER multimillion-dollar contract from the Trump administration," Warren said in an April 23 social media post. "This looks like corruption in plain sight."
Eric Trump didn't respond to requests for comment. His spokesperson recently told the Financial Times that Eric Trump had "no involvement in Foundation's management, operations, strategic decisions or commercial activities, including the solicitation, negotiation, procurement or execution of any government contracts."
While the Eric Trump announcement created speculation within Foundation that a Democratic-led Congress may look to investigate the company, Foundation itself didn't actually win the $24 million in contracts, despite that assertion being widely reported across news outlets.
Instead, it acquired Florida-based Boardwalk Robotics in late 2024, and government research contracts won by that firm account for the claim, said a person with knowledge of the matter. Foundation used Boardwalk's robot Alex as the basis for its first robot, the Phantom MK-1, this person said.
Foundation's deal for Boardwalk included performance milestones for the robot that haven't been reached, said a separate person with direct knowledge of the deal.
In 2024, CNBC reported that letters Pathak sent to prospective investors cited an imminent investment and $300 million purchase order from General Motors , claims the automaker rejected.
Foundation co-founder Mike LeBlanc said at the time he was "embarrassed" about the marketing materials.
Insiders fret that Foundation could soon fold if Pathak doesn't secure fresh funding. Pathak has been seeking to raise hundreds of millions of dollars at a $3 billion valuation since at least January.
Pathak is Foundation's sole board member, a structure that has raised concerns among prospective investors about corporate governance, said the people familiar with the matter. He also owns most of the firm's shares.
That setup allowed Pathak to borrow $4.6 million last year, which he called a short-term loan at the time, the people said. Existing investors are aware of the loan through the company's financial disclosures, the people said.
"This is what happens in a company with no governance," said one of the people. "Are you just going to let it ride into the ground, and you ride off into the sunset?"
Foundation also ran out of cash for payroll in August, though employees only had to wait about two days to get paid after the company secured a bridge loan from an existing investor, the people said.
Pathak told employees this week in a memo that he was working on sourcing money to pay back wages.
The company was founded in April 2024 by Pathak, Tribe Capital CEO Arjun Sethi and LeBlanc, co-founder of Cobalt Robotics, a maker of autonomous security guards, according to a fundraising pitch at the time.
Foundation went on to hire dozens of robotics engineers and artificial intelligence experts, managing to lure some from Tesla and Amazon -owned autonomous vehicle company Zoox.
Before Foundation, Pathak was known as the founder of Synapse, a kind of middleman that enabled fintech firms like Mercury , Dave and YieldStreet to offer savings accounts and credit cards with the help of small community banks.
Synapse was a behind-the-scenes player until its collapse left more than 100,000 Americans with a combined $265 million in deposits locked out of their FDIC-backed accounts.
While some customers received partial payments during Synapse's bankruptcy proceedings, thousands remain without access to their money after more than two years. A bankruptcy trustee, the former FDIC chair Jelena McWilliams , said as much as $96 million in customer funds went missing.
The bankruptcy proceedings concluded last year without uncovering where the funds went; Pathak blamed a banking partner named Evolve, and Evolve blamed Synapse for the mess. U.S. regulators didn't intervene until the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau sued Synapse last year, opening up a $55 million fund for customer relief.
Pathak withdrew $320,000 in loans from Synapse as it spiraled toward bankruptcy in 2024 amid disputes over unmatched ledgers, according to the consultant and independent journalist Jason Mikula.
Federal prosecutors convened a grand jury to investigate possible criminal misconduct at Synapse, the Wall Street Journal reported last year. The WSJ report didn't mention Pathak specifically.
The controversy didn't dissuade Eric Trump from investing in Foundation and Pathak, who he called a friend in the April broadcast interview.
"I walked into his factory, and I couldn't believe what I saw," Eric Trump said . "I'm telling you, he's doing a phenomenal job."

articles.title_orig: China holds 80% of underwater data center patents in past 20 years, can boost AI energy use
articles.title_zh: China holds 80% of underwater data center patents in past 20 years, can boost AI energy use
articles.content_orig:
China owns around 80 percent of all global underwater data center patents.
Two Chinese researchers analyzing 168 patents filed between 2006 and 2026 reported this finding.
They also found that China holds the lion's share, with South Korea owning around 17, and the rest split between the US and Europe.
A new study has found that China owns around 80 percent of all global underwater data center patents. That’s not to say China owns much of the technology used in these setups, but it does reveal how active it has been in patenting in this field.
The study’s findings come from two Chinese researchers analyzing 168 patents filed between 2006 and 2026. It appears to show that technological focus has shifted quite dramatically over this time.
Before about 2014, patents were dominated by American, Norwegian, and Canadian researchers exploring underwater enclosures and pressure protection. Between about 2015 and 2020, attention turned to cooling, electrical supply, and long-term reliability.
From 2021, Chinese researchers became the dominant source for patents, particularly focusing on modular construction and maintenance. They also found that China holds the lion’s share, with South Korea owning around 17, and the rest split between the US and Europe.
Chinese patents in particular focus on the actual construction, installation, connections, and maintenance of them at scale. This appears to show that China is shifting focus to the more practical elements rather than proving experimental technology.
All very interesting, but why all the interest? Well, data centers generate an enormous amount of heat when in operation. This comes from the conversion of electricity into heat by the vast number of computer processors.
Typically, this is handled by using a combination of fans, chillers, cooling towers, and liquid-cooling systems to manage temperatures. That is costly in terms of hardware and additional electricity costs.
If the centers could be placed underwater, they could take advantage of the ocean’s near-limitless supply of very cold seawater. Obviously, you can’t just submerge the hardware directly into the ocean, so they need to be placed inside sealed, pressure-resistant containers first.
These are then lowered and secured to the seabed, and connections are made to the shore for power and data cables. Once there, the heat from the servers can be transferred to the cold ocean water using special internal cooling systems.
To this end, the seawater acts as a massive heat sink, potentially eliminating much of the mechanical cooling equipment needed on land. This doesn’t make the computers themselves consume less electricity, but it can reduce the energy spent keeping them cool.
And it is not just a theoretical technology either. Famously, Microsoft deployed one, called Project Natick , off the coast of Scotland in 2018. The project ran for around two years, and results were very encouraging.
According to Microsoft, the underwater data center had just one-eighth of the failure rate of similar land-based setups. Yet despite this, Microsoft chose not to commercialize the technology, and confirmed in 2024 that the project had been discontinued.
So, is the 80 percent figure something other nations should sit up and take notice of? Yes, and no. It is clear China has established some kind of lead here in terms of patents, but the engineering challenges of actually deploying them are enormous.
The shift in focus to modularity likely reflects China’s ambitions to scale the technology commercially. But it is important to note that patents tend to be territorial in nature.
Holding a large share of patents in a particular field doesn’t automatically give a country control of the technology worldwide.
Christopher graduated from Cardiff University in 2004 with a Masters Degree in Geology. Since then, he has worked exclusively within the Built Environment, Occupational Health and Safety and Environmental Consultancy industries. He is a qualified and accredited Energy Consultant, Green Deal Assessor and Practitioner member of IEMA. Chris’s main interests range from Science and Engineering, Military and Ancient History to Politics and Philosophy.

articles.title_orig: Restaurant chain may rethink controversial 20% service charge in some venues after customer pushback
articles.title_zh: Restaurant chain may rethink controversial 20% service charge in some venues after customer pushback
articles.content_orig:
Billy Downs, president of Ford's Garage, tells Fox News Digital the challenges of balancing employee compensation with affordability for diners as select Florida franchise locations experiment with a different approach to covering labor expenses.
Ford's Garage may be reconsidering a controversial policy that automatically adds a 20% service charge to customers' checks at five Florida restaurants, with the chain's president acknowledging that some diners are unhappy with the mandatory fee.
In an interview with Fox News Digital, Billy Downs said the policy, which is being tested by one franchisee at five Florida locations, remains under review.
"I think that we need to listen to the consumer on those things, to be honest with you," Downs said. "So, we are, and we may be encouraging a change to that program."
RESTAURANT 'ADMIN' FEES SPARK BACKLASH AS DINERS QUESTION WHAT THEY'RE PAYING FOR
Marc Brown, president of franchisee 23 Restaurant Services, told Fox News Digital the program has been largely successful, resulting in higher wages for employees without alienating most customers.
"Our servers in the locations that run our service charge program are making significantly higher average hourly pay than our servers and bartenders in locations that do not have it," Brown said.
A Ford's Garage franchisee in Florida (not pictured) has an automatic 20% service charge on all checks in lieu of tipping. (Peter Burke/Fox News Digital)
The policy is part of a team service model introduced by 23 Restaurant Services, which operates Ford's Garage restaurants throughout Florida.
Rather than relying on traditional tipping, the model automatically adds a 20% service charge to each check to support a commission-based compensation structure.
Servers and bartenders earn commissions based on sales, while the model is also designed to provide more equitable compensation for kitchen and support staff, according to the franchisee's website.
EX-WAITRESS REVEALS RESTAURANT TIPPING SECRET MOST CUSTOMERS DON'T REALIZE — EXPERT CALLS IT 'BAD HOSPITALITY'
Additional tips are optional.
Downs said the experiment was intended to explore whether a different compensation model could help control costs while rewarding employees for their service.
"It certainly was a test to see if this can help keep the cost down to the consumer, as well as reward the server," he said.
Billy Downs, president of Ford's Garage, told Fox News Digital the company "may be encouraging a change" to the test program. (Fox News Digital)
The Ford's Garage location in Plantation near Fort Lauderdale is among the restaurants that have implemented the policy "in lieu of a traditional gratuity ," according to its website. That location also adds a separate 1% entertainment fee assessed by the shopping center.
"This fee is passed directly to the retail center, is not a gratuity and is not retained by Ford's Garage or distributed to employees," the website states.
APPLEBEE'S CUSTOMER PUSHES BACK ON SUGGESTED TIP AFTER CHECKING THE MATH
Brown said the service charge is disclosed to customers multiple times verbally and in writing before they order, giving them the choice of whether to dine there.
"So, to us, it's no different than just charging a higher price on the menu," he said.
Most guests aren't bothered by the fee, Brown said, "because they like the Ford's Garage experience."
The president of 23 Restaurant Services said most customers aren't bothered by the fee "because they like the Ford's Garage experience." (Peter Burke/Fox News Digital)
But Downs acknowledged the policy has produced some controversy.
"There's been some big wins, and there's been consumers that just do not want to pay a service charge," he said.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS
The experiment comes as restaurant operators grapple with rising labor costs and changes to tipped minimum wages.
"But the biggest pushback is people don't want to have a mandated service charge, and I get it," Downs said. "You know, I'm not sure I want it either in certain times."
"We have not made any decisions, but we talk about it regularly."
Brown, however, said the criticism appears to come from a relatively small percentage of diners, noting that most participating restaurants have experienced year-over-year growth after operating under the model for multiple years.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER
He also rejected the notion that an automatic service charge diminishes a server or bartender's incentive to provide quality hospitality, saying employees are expected to "provide great service to every guest regardless of what they expect to get in terms of additional tip."
Under the model implemented at select Ford's Garage locations, tipping is optional. (iStock)
Founded in Fort Myers in 2012, Ford's Garage has grown to 36 restaurants across nine states. Downs said the chain has prioritized affordability, with an average customer check of about $26 and weekday value meals starting at $10.99.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
Downs, who previously spoke to Fox News Digital about the chain's emphasis on old-fashioned hospitality , said providing consistently good service can help address customer concerns.
"If you give great service all the time, that can help to eliminate problems," Downs said.
As for whether the service-charge policy could change, Brown said discussions are ongoing.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"We have not made any decisions, but we talk about it regularly," he said.
Peter Burke is a lifestyle editor with Fox News Digital. He covers various lifestyle topics, with an emphasis on food and drink.

articles.title_orig: No Pilots. Few Air Traffic Controllers. What Could Go Wrong?
articles.title_zh: No Pilots. Few Air Traffic Controllers. What Could Go Wrong?
articles.content_orig:
On September 27, US transportation secretary Sean Duffy posted a video on X with the words “GAME CHANGER.” “Introducing ‘SMART’—the new air traffic management tool that saves YOU time, cuts back DELAYS, and makes your flying experience BETTER,” he wrote. This was a new AI-infused air traffic control system. Almost three weeks later, that post would get a new life, as a nervous joke, as the FAA issued a national groundstop on Friday the 13th that instantly threw the world’s airline schedules into chaos. The administration quickly announced that there was no evidence of a cyberattack, and no sign that SMART had anything to do with the communications failure at the heart of the government’s decision to suspend flights. But when asked on Friday night whether he could definitively rule out AI failure, Homeland Security secretary Markwayne Mullin could only say, “There’s nothing certain right now.”
New systems like SMART are only the tip of the iceberg when it comes to the AI aviation revolution currently underway. Take, for instance, the Cessna Caravan that took off from Buchanan Field Airport in Concord, California, and flew south to Phoenix on a calm September morning. The plane, a single-engine turboprop, then turned east to Fort Worth, stopped at Shaw Air Force Base in South Carolina, and finally arrived at Dare County Regional Airport off the coast of North Carolina. The zigzag, coast-to-coast trip covered 3,200 miles; along the way, the aircraft navigated busy airspace and maneuvered to avoid storms.
None of this would be remarkable, save for one fact: The entire journey took place without a single human hand touching the plane’s controls.
According to Joby Aviation, the company that carried out the project, a safety pilot was aboard the Cessna at all times—but never needed to intervene. The pilotless trip marked a major milestone in aviation. The air travel industry has long been technologically conservative, and with good reason: When human lives are at stake, it’s better to be time-tested and a little dated than cutting-edge and unpredictable. But AI is making inroads into aviation with unprecedented speed. The effects now are hard to see, but the changes in the offing are huge, promising to remake the economics of air travel and transform how people and things move around in the sky. A big question remains, though: Can we trust this technology to be reliable and safe?
Depends who you ask. “We're introducing all this new technology to improve the system, and it's going to be a disaster,” says a recently retired FAA employee. “This is literally a Pandora's box that we are going to regret.”
Aviation’s embrace of AI traces back to the early 2000s, when advances in batteries and microelectronics suddenly made drones much more capable and inexpensive. The surge convinced officials that robots and humans would eventually need to share the airways, and that new infrastructure would be necessary to allow that. At the time, virtually all aircraft were human-piloted, and there was no way for drones to avoid human-flown planes or each other.
In 2007, the federal government rolled out a sweeping project called Next Generation Air Transportation System—NextGen, for short—that mandated broad changes to the air travel system over the decades to come. Among its provisions was the requirement that, by 2020, aircraft in the United States be equipped with ADS-B, a system that constantly sends radio signals telling everyone in the vicinity where you are and where you’re headed.
Joby’s aircraft flying past Lower Manhattan, New York, in April.
With a road map to robot-friendly skies in place, big players like Amazon and Walmart began working on ambitious plans for drone delivery services. In 2014, Google unveiled Project Wing, a drone delivery offering that by 2018 was ferrying food, coffee, and medication to 164 homes near Canberra, Australia . The next year, the pilot program was expanded to Christiansburg, Virginia . Costs were high and service slow, but those early programs weren’t meant to become viable businesses. Instead, they were providing Google with operational experience for the years to come.
Around the same time, a host of startups began working on a related kind of vehicle: electric vertical takeoff and landing aircraft, or eVTOLs, also known as electric air taxis. These are, essentially, oversized drones (with room for pilots, for now) designed to carry a small number of people a short distance. By 2022 there were 600 different models under development. Soon, their manufacturers promised, cheap, short aerial hops would be commonplace. Joby was among those leading the charge: In 2020, the company unveiled the design of its S4 model, which it said would be able to carry a pilot and four passengers 100 miles or more at speeds of up to 200 mph. The S4’s maiden flight took place last year.
A commercial launch seemed just around the corner . But deadlines kept getting pushed back . As it turned out, engineering a flying autonomous robot was just part of the overall problem. You also needed to design an airspace that they could operate in, train humans to pilot or supervise them, develop an economic framework within which they could earn money, and so on. “It's a very important, safe, careful dance,” says Bowles.
Silicon Valley’s speed has long been in conflict with air travel norms. “Aviation regulation has been conservative and prioritizes reliability, because the consequences of failure are severe,” says Mary Schiavo, an aviation lawyer and former inspector general in the Department of Transportation. “Certification standards and airworthiness require proof and demonstrated safety, and that usually means incremental rather than radical change.” The FAA was in no rush to let unproven robots go careening around the national airspace.
AI faced another kind of resistance in Europe. In 2017, aircraft manufacturers Airbus and Dassault asked the EASA , the European Union’s version of the FAA, to consider allowing airliners to operate with a single pilot in the cockpit. Traditionally, airliners require multiple pilots to divide the considerable workload of flying a plane and to ensure that if one pilot becomes incapacitated, the other can carry on. In Airbus’ vision, automated systems would shoulder the copilot’s workload and even take over entirely if needed.
That idea horrified pilots. The European Cockpit Association, a union of airline pilots, lodged a strong protest. Such a move “would remove an independent safety professional from the flight deck and give operators greater influence over the safety judgments that a pilot would otherwise make,” the union explained to me in an email. Last year, EASA shelved the plan.
Nevertheless, AI pressed onward. In 2023, the FAA began issuing waivers to allow delivery-drone flights beyond the visual range of operators; by the end of this year it could make the rule change permanent. Some of the biggest players are already pushing ahead aggressively. This past August, Amazon announced that it planned to expand its drone delivery service to 500 locations across the country by the end of the year. Walmart is planning drone delivery from 270 store locations by the end of 2027.
The ultimate goal is far larger. Industry insiders say that in a maximal vision of the technology’s build-out, hundreds of thousands of drones will be servicing most or all of the US population. “In five to 10 years, it’s going to be completely ubiquitous,” Anthony Vittone, chief operating officer of the drone technology company DroneUp, told me in a story for Sherwood News last year . “People are going to be, like, ‘I don’t know how I lived without it.’”
Joby and other eVTOL companies haven’t progressed quite as fast, but they, too, are moving ahead. In April, Joby flew the first-ever point-to-point eVTOL flight within New York City, from John F. Kennedy Airport to three heliports in Manhattan. The company has carried out similar flights in California

articles.title_orig: The Surprise Censorship Battle Over My Cocktail Book Has Left Me Shaken—and Stirred
articles.title_zh: The Surprise Censorship Battle Over My Cocktail Book Has Left Me Shaken—and Stirred
articles.content_orig:
DEAR ABBY : My sister-in-law “Leah” has been a poor money manager all her life. She is in significant credit card debt and had to borrow money to help pay for her wedding, despite the fact that she has been a teacher for decades. She has never been a saver — always a spender.
When my husband passed away recently, he left me with $1 million in life insurance proceeds. When Leah found out about it (I’m not sure how), she asked me to lend her some money to get back on her feet. When I refused, my other sister-in-law chastised me, saying that my husband would have lent her the money. Leah has been bailed out a few times by her sister but never by my husband. Am I wrong to stand my ground? — NOT AN ENABLER
DEAR NOT AN ENABLER : My heart goes out to you for the loss of your husband. Leah may be using the word “lend,” but believe me when I say you would never see that money again. If she wants to get out of debt, she needs to speak to a credit counselor, not her brother’s grieving widow. If she brings it up again, tell her to visit the National Foundation for Credit Counseling at nfcc.org.
DEAR ABBY : I am a 70-year-old divorced man. For the past 10 years, my ex-wife has been living with me. Due to her medical condition and lack of family support, she has no one else to assist her. My own health is declining, so caring for her is a physical strain and emotionally stressful. She refuses any suggestion of a senior living facility because her only income is a small Social Security benefit.
How do I move on without fighting and accusations? I know I facilitated this by allowing her into my home in the first place. Any ideas where to begin? — FRUSTRATED IN TEXAS
DEAR FRUSTRATED : You were kind to take in and care for your ex a decade ago, but this arrangement is now affecting your health. To protect your own well-being, you must put your foot down. Help your ex-wife one last time by finding her a facility she can afford. Do not expect the transition to be pleasant, but the result will be an improvement for both of you.
DEAR ABBY : I am a happily married woman who went through a midlife crisis more than 20 years ago. At the time, I left my husband for another man, who gave me an expensive cocktail ring. When my relationship with the new man started to suffer for various reasons, I returned to my husband. Our marriage has remained strong ever since.
I have never worn the ring and have always felt guilty for having it. Should I contact my former lover and return it? Should I pawn it and send him the proceeds? Or maybe you have another suggestion? — RINGS HOLLOW IN ARIZONA
DEAR RINGS HOLLOW : Sell the ring and donate the proceeds to a worthy charitable cause. Do not open the door to further contact with your former lover.
Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren. For nearly four decades, Jeanne Phillips penned this column, which was founded in 1956 by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at http://www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 270135, Kansas City, MO 64127.

articles.title_orig: Is indigenous science really science? (and its connection to AI)
articles.title_zh: Is indigenous science really science? (and its connection to AI)
articles.content_orig:
Well, both of the world’s most prestigious science journals have gone off the rails, a fact confirmed again when I read the Science editorial and letter below on AI and indigenous science, which then led me to a Perspective in Nature on “two eyed seeing” in neuroscience. As you know, the two-eyed metaphor refers to the claimed salubrious effects of blending “indigenous science” with “Western science” (the latter is now known as “science”.)
The point of the Science editorial above is simply this: because indigenous knowledge (and I define “knowledge” as “justified true belief”) is not widely represented in publications or writings that can be accessed by AI, so it is not found very often in searches.  Thus, as Running Horse Collin says, there “cannot be an indigenous AI within the current AI framework.”
There are problems of translation, too:
Additionally, AI models would have to be trained in translating Indigenous science vocabulary between languages. This is not impossible, but Indigenous languages reflect multidimensional scientific principles and concepts and how they work together. Language and context would have to be translated into those of the linear world of Western science. That is not presently possible. Moreover, AI is trained to reference Western scientific data and concepts as the “control” for the interpretation of concepts. Thus, it would evaluate Indigenous concepts, data, and frameworks against Western methodologies to determine validity, accuracy, or meaning.
Finally, the biggest problem is one that reflects how modern science’s “ways of knowing” aren’t the same as indigenous “ways of knowing.” This is a problem that I’ve discussed extensively with reference to Mātauranga Māori (henceforth “MM”), the Māori “way of knowing” that is the subject of a battle in New Zealand about what counts as science. From the paper above:
The major, overarching problem is that in Western science, the purpose of research is to obtain and convey information, whereas in Indigenous science, information must come with a purpose. Within the Lakota scientific system, for example, the point of conducting innovation, experiments, or research must align with ethics and the foundational scientific purpose, which is to preserve all life and work within it. This is a very different way to understand the acquisition, protection, and use of knowledge. In its current form and design, AI is effectively the outcome of multiple permutations of statistical calculations conveying statistically weighted output and trained to generate practical outcomes. However, within Indigenous scientific systems, there is no “right answer” without an initial, ethically aligned purpose and process. Therefore, “what is the point” is the point.
There’s more to indigenous “ways of knowing” than just obtaining knowledge under an ethical system, though. As in MM, indigenous “science” nearly always incorporates things that modern science—it’s called “Western science” in the article—doesn’t deal with qua science. These are things like ethics, religious codes, spiritual matters (as in spiritual healing), folklore, tradition, and so on.
I’m not denying that indigenous people can acquire knowledge through trial and error, as they have with navigation in Polynesia or growing mussels in New Zealand.  Nor do I deny that these observations can lead to substantial medical or scientific advances.  Three examples are the use of willow bark to relieve pain (leading to the development of aspirin), the use of cinchona bark to relieve fevers (leading to the development of quinine to mitigate malarial symptoms), and the use of plant-derived curare as arrow poison (leading to advances in anesthesia and muscle relaxants). These all came from knowledge acquired by indigenous (or pre-Caucasion) people.
But it’s not just “colonized” and oppressed people (a theme of all three documents) who have folk wisdom.  Remember that the development of the smallpox vaccine by Jenner was prompted by the observation that English milkmaids who had gotten cowpox were immune to smallpox. This led to Edward Jenner’s development of a smallpox vaccine (the first vaccine ever) and the rise of immunology.  But Jenner was successful because he tested the folk observations using methods now more refined in modern science: hypothesis testing and repeated observations with the subjects being blinded.
The point I want to make here is that folk observations can be a foundation for modern science, or even be incorporated into modern science. But they only become part of modern science when they are tested. Jenner published his repeated tests on the vaccine in 1798, and the use of salicylic acid and quinine were isolated, tested and reported on in the mid-18th century.  That is when the scientific advances occurred, although again, they were derived from folk observations.
But remember that there are many parts of indigenous “ways of knowing” that do not comprise knowledge in the modern scientific sense. There are many herbal cures that don’t work, and don’t forget all the ineffective spiritual cures that are part of MM and other indigenous “systems of knowledge”.  There is a well-funded branch of the NIH, the National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health, that has tested folk and indigenous remedies using modern blind controlled trials. Almost without exception, “folk wisdom” was not substantiated scientifically .  A few examples are given in the linked 2009 article:
Ten years ago the government set out to test herbal and other alternative health remedies to find the ones that work. After spending $2.5 billion, the disappointing answer seems to be that almost none of them do.
Echinacea for colds. Ginkgo biloba for memory. Glucosamine and chondroitin for arthritis. Black cohosh for menopausal hot flashes. Saw palmetto for prostate problems. Shark cartilage for cancer. All proved no better than dummy pills in big studies funded by the National Center for Complementary and Alternative Medicine. The lone exception: ginger capsules may help chemotherapy nausea.
As for therapies, acupuncture has been shown to help certain conditions, and yoga, massage, meditation and other relaxation methods may relieve symptoms like pain, anxiety and fatigue.
However, the government also is funding studies of purported energy fields, distance healing and other approaches that have little if any biological plausibility or scientific evidence.
The point is not to denigrate indigenous knowledge, but to show that any folk “knowledge” not tested with the methods of modern science cannot be regarded as “knowledge.”
And that brings me to the main point: there is not “indigenous science” and “Western science” that stand as separate entities, much less coequal entities . There is scientific knowledge and there are folk assertions, and that is all there is. It is telling that Running Horse Collin,  a member of the Oglala Lakota Nation, does not tell us what indigenous science comprises beyond pointing out its differences from “Western science” (see below)
And that is the second point: indigenous science is said to be different from “Western science” in ways that make the former, in several respects,  a complementary and salubrious way of knowing . That feeds into the metaphor of “two-eyed seeing”: the claim that you find out a lot more things if you simultaneously look at nature from the “Western” perspective and the indigenous perspective. Here is a figure from the Nature paper below implying a coequality (or at least a substantial contribution) of both eyes, even though in reality one eye sees a much wider landscape than the other:
Another point: examples of major contributions to human knowledge made by indigenous groups are rarely given in papers touting “other ways of knowing” . The paper by Running Horse Collin is a case in point. She cites only one example (my bolding)
Yet, these differences do not mean that Indigenous knowledge is irrelevant to the pr

articles.title_orig: We Asked Vogue, GQ, and a Pro Stylist to Kill Jensen Huang’s Leather Jacket
articles.title_zh: We Asked Vogue, GQ, and a Pro Stylist to Kill Jensen Huang’s Leather Jacket
articles.content_orig:
Jensen Huang’s midlife-crisis makeover hasn’t helped the Nvidia CEO’s image this week. In a matter of days, Huang’s questionable sartorial leanings have shifted wildly from wannabe cool Harley dad to low-down leather Lothario . Fashion moves fast, but even in the style world, this is a breakneck volte-face .
As Emma Childs wonderfully observed in The Cut, “a $9,000 leather moto is not the outerwear of a man faithfully going home to his wife and kids after a long day of architecting the AI revolution.” And since Huang’s tomfoolery has managed to spank more than $1 trillion in less than a month, something has to be done.
This is where WIRED comes to the rescue, aided by Vogue, GQ and a celebrity stylist, no less. We’ve charted the menacing glow-up of tech bros before, but merely observing the worrying trend back in 2025 is clearly no longer enough. It’s time to roll up our Armani sleeves and help.
“Tech bros were total nerds before," says Karen Clarkson , a professional stylist whose clients have included Nike, Google, Apple, Calvin Klein, and Vivienne Westwood. "Fashion didn’t touch their lives at all. They didn’t have style.” Pictures of Huang’s pre-biker fashion-vacuum days certainly bear this out. “Then, like [Jeff] Bezos, they all stepped up . And there’s a rivalry that’s come with that, whether it’s the fashion makeover, the grooming, the skin treatments, or gym regimen. Now we have Mark Zuckerberg in the front row at Prada .”
Jensen Huang’s Banished Biker Look 1! (clockwise from top left): Giorgio Armani long-sleeved cashmere polo, $1,695 ; Lemaire workwear jacket, $1,050 ; The Row Nesper pant, $1,250 ; Giorgio Armani leather slippers, $1,850 ; Speciale cotton-mix stripe shirt; £295 .
As a man clearly in dress distress, where better to start than with Murray Clark, head of editorial at British GQ . Controversially, Clark has a radical notion that Huang should keep clothing matters as they are. “I’d argue that Jensen Huang stays exactly how he is because this is who he is—a coiffed, leather-jacket wearing, mistake-making middle-aged man for all the world to see.”
Before publicly admitting on Sunday to having an affair with a businesswoman who US intelligence says is also a Chinese spy, in 2024, Huang confessed onstage that his wife, Lori, suggested and chose his biker outfits for him because he found most other fabrics “itchy.”
If Jensen keeps his jackets (he apparently owns 30 to 40), Clarkson thinks that Huang might even find himself on the catwalk. “If he wants to go down that route, then for sure Demna [Gucci’s creative director] would have him walking in his next show in Milan,” she says. “But he’s very Arnold Schwarzenegger and the Terminator with his black leathers, which is a bit close to the bone, really, with AI and that humanity is potentially doomed . I don’t know if he’s wise to lean into Arnie too heavily.”
Jensen Huang’s Banished Biker Look 2! (clockwise from top left): The Row Vana jacket, $12,000 ; Speciale lambswool crew, £435 ; The Row Victor shirt, $1,290 ; Lemaire Rail Belt, $320 ; John Lobb City II New Standard shoes, $1,878 ; The Row Paulo corduroy pant, $1,590 .
Let’s get some sage advice, then, from Chioma Nnadi, head of editorial at British Vogue . “If I were styling Jensen Huang, I’d advise him to cleanse the palate entirely, ditch the rock and roll shrunken leather jackets for something more somber,” Nnadi says. “A collared Oxford shirt and a navy or gray crewneck jumper would do the trick and wouldn’t read as aggressively corporate as a traditional suit. The message needs to be ‘I’m a serious person, and I’m leaving that tragic try-hard boomer dad wardrobe behind along with my despicable behavior.’”
Clarkson agrees, saying that while the term “unapologetic” is often used in fashion, in this instance, Huang needs a more apologetic dress code, moving away from anything too flashy. So out go the overtly sexual Tom Ford leathers—which Jensen can handily sell off for $1 million a pop to his Huang-boys to offset any alimony outlays that may, or may not, be coming his way—and in come understated and neutral tones.
“He could take a leaf out of Harry Styles’ dress down codes and check The Row for minimal looks,” Clarkson says. “A Lemaire workwear jacket is also a good vibe. It shows he’s willing to put in the work to win back his family. Also, since he’s spoken about feeling itchy, maybe he should repent a bit and wear lambswool instead of cashmere.”
Jensen Huang's Banished Biker Look 3! (clockwise from top left): Paul Smith Ripstop field jacket, $1,025 ; Brunello Cucinelli alpaca-blend sweater, $3,400 ; The Row Sue pant, $2,300 ; Paul Smith Garson shoes, $475 .
Asking Clarkson to step away from her celebrity clients for a moment to perform a hasty hypothetical make under (or glow down?) for Huang, she has very kindly put together three outfits that I think we can all agree give off considerably fewer bad-egg biker vibes with pieces from Paul Smith, The Row, Lemaire, Giorgio Armani, Brunello Cucinelli, and more. If you’re lucky enough to have a budget to match Huang's, we’ve added links to the individual pieces in the captions under each “look.”
“There’s been a lot of tight-fitted leather jackets that just about cover his biceps, which always feels like he’s looking to lure his next lover or like he’s just whizzed off on his Ducati to have a quick lunchtime visit with his mistress,” says Clarkson. “That’s not the vibe you want to go before Congress with.” For the Hill, she suggests Huang go for a Nehru collar that “feels a bit more buttoned up.”
Giorgio Armani's Spring-Summer 2027 show in Milan.
However, because Huang’s existing look is so strong, Clarkson advises that changing it too quickly will not only draw an enormous amount of commentary but even more memes . “Little steps, not a full overnight makeover. That’s why he should perhaps keep the leather jacket, something like a suede blouson instead of the biker,” she says, adding that the black jeans should be ditched in favor of proper pants.
“He could do a tie as well—a bit more apologetic, a bit more formal, a bit more respectful. So a brown leather jacket with a tie and a shirt—so then it’s a segue into a new direction,” Clarkson says, citing Giorgio Armani’s June Milan collection as ideal inspiration.
However, Clarkson says credit must ultimately go to Lori Huang, Jensen’s wife of 41 years. “She did a brilliant job. If anyone comes out of this as a winner, it’s her. She could rebrand as a Hollywood stylist at this point because she’s done a great job of creating an identity for her husband. Almost too good because it’s attracted too many women. Still, she could step away with a really great divorce settlement and a whole new career.”

articles.title_orig: NYC is spending $70 million on 5 city-run grocery stores pricing essentials 30% below retail
articles.title_zh: NYC is spending $70 million on 5 city-run grocery stores pricing essentials 30% below retail
articles.content_orig:
A group of New York City supermarkets claim the cityâs plan to operate five subsidized grocery stores will offer such artificially low prices that no competitor in normal circumstances could ever charge or maintain.
MANHATTAN (CN) â Attorneys for New York City told a Manhattan federal judge Thursday they are confident that Mayor Zohran Mamdaniâs plan for city-run, discounted supermarkets is sound against civil antitrust claims from a coalition of local grocers who claim the campaign promise amounts to anticompetitive business practices.
Mamdani announced in July the âCore Basketâ set of kitchen staples covered by the cityâs guaranteed 30% discount would include all fresh produce, meat, and seafood, in addition to 20 other essential items like cheese, milk and bread.
A group of large independent grocery stores in the city, led by the National Supermarket Association, sued the city in September, claiming the tax-financed municipal stores rely on predatory pricing that will drive the unsubsidized local grocers out of business.
The plaintiffs ask U.S. District Judge Jennifer Rochon impose a preliminary injunction, under Section 2 of the Sherman Act which prohibits attempted monopolization and conspiracy to monopolize, and to halt the cityâs selection of a private operator to manage daily operations while litigation progresses.
Attorneys for the city on Thursday however argued Rochon, a Joe Biden appointee in the Southern District of New York, could dismiss the motion for preliminary injunction for lack of irreparable harm to the plaintiffs absent the injunction.
The city says the program is designed to improve affordability and consumer welfare, and certainly will not harm consumers.
âThe program is intended to be complementary to existing food retailers, not to replace existing food retailers,â Daniel Kuo Crandall, a lawyer for New York City Law Departmentâs commercial and real estate litigation division, said during oral arguments.
An injunction delaying the rollout of the cityâs first two discounted grocery stores, Crandall said, would instead cause concrete and definite harm to food-insecure and lower income New Yorkers.
The plaintiffs claim Mamdaniâs plan poses an âunprecedentedâ risk of anticompetitive monopolization, but the city argued Thursday that competition between the public and private sector is still competition.
âCompetition between the public and private sector can still benefit consumers and still be the type of competition that is supposed to be protected by the antitrust laws, and certainly should not be inhibited by any of the antitrust laws,â Crandall said.
The city noted it does not intend for the five stores to have deli counters, butcher counters or other specialty items that other grocers carry, and will encourage New Yorkers to continue to visit other local food retailers for freshly prepared food.
Mamdani has said New York families shopping at the cityâs markets would save an estimated $90 on grocery bills each month, totaling over $1,000 annually.
City-owned grocery stores were one of the key promises Mamdani, a self-described democratic socialist, centered his historic 2025 mayoral campaign on.
The city has committed $70 million in municipal capital funding for construction and fit-out of the five stores.
Richard Lawson, from the America First Policy Institute, argued Thursday that the cityâs mandated discount runs afoul of predatory pricing provisions of federal antitrust law, designed to protect marketplace competition.
Rochon did not rule on the preliminary injunction motion from the bench.
The first two stores are planned for East Harlem and Hunts Point in the Bronx. The Bronx store, a redevelopment project at the site of the former Spofford Juvenile Detention Facility, is targeted to open first sometime next year, with a goal of no later than the end of 2027.
The National Supermarket Association claims about 20 existing grocery stores will be affected given their proximity to the Hunts Point site in the Bronx, while 26 businesses are in range of the site in the more densely populated neighborhood of East Harlem.
This lawsuit is the second filed over the municipal grocery store initiative. The Multicultural Business Coalition, a group representing the owners of smaller grocery stores and bodega corner stores, brought a class action in August in Manhattan Supreme Court similarly challenging the plan’s potential affects on competitors.

articles.title_orig: Finland rejects reported Russian demand to leave NATO as part of peace talks
articles.title_zh: Finland rejects reported Russian demand to leave NATO as part of peace talks
articles.content_orig:
Finland has rejected a reported Russian demand that it leave NATO as part of Ukraine peace talks, with Defense Minister Antti Häkkänen saying its membership in the alliance wasn’t up for negotiation.
"Such matters are in no way a matter for negotiation. Russia knows that. This is absolutely outrageous to even suggest such a thing," Häkkänen told reporters on Friday , according to Finnish broadcaster Yle. Finland, which shares a 1,340-kilometer border with Russia, joined NATO in 2023 in a foreign policy U-turn prompted by the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
German newspaper Bild reported that a Russian proposal made during talks in Abu Dhabi this week included Moscow keeping occupied Ukrainian territories, gaining control of new swathes of land, demilitarizing ports in Ukraine, removing NATO bases from the Baltics, and Finland leaving NATO.
Russia proposed withdrawing its nuclear weapons from Belarus and refraining from stationing intermediate-range missiles there in exchange, Bild reported.
But it remains unclear which proposals Russian President Vladimir Putin would support after discussions between intermediaries, according to the report.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said a new security framework for Europe for after the war raised by the Americans “can be dangerous."
“Russia certainly cannot make decisions on behalf of all the societies that are members of NATO,” he told reporters on Friday.
Zelenskyy’s comments were not in direct response to the demands reported by Bild, but came after a meeting between Zelenskyy and U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner on Thursday in Dublin .
“Putin's desire to change borders in Europe is a fact. I am sure this is part of his concept of revising security guarantees in Europe. This is dangerous because, in my view, it is precisely things like this that lead to wars or escalations,” Zelenskyy said.

articles.title_orig: Trump to hold trilateral talks with Xi, Putin in China next week: White House
articles.title_zh: Trump to hold trilateral talks with Xi, Putin in China next week: White House
articles.content_orig:
US President Donald Trump will meet Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin in China next week for trilateral talks on the sidelines of the APEC summit, the White House said Friday.
The meeting will take place in Shenzhen.
"The President has made it clear that, among other topics, he will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world, whose proliferation President Trump believes is very dangerous," Assistant Press Secretary Olivia Wales told reporters on a call.
Trump will also hold a bilateral meeting and working lunch with Xi on Thursday afternoon before concluding his visit to China with the trilateral meeting, Wales said.
A senior US official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said Washington does not expect an agreement to emerge from the talks.
"I would characterize this as the entry point, the first conversation, certainly at the leader level between these countries," the official said.
The official said China's nuclear arsenal is "growing by far the fastest in the world" and argued that it was time for Beijing to "step up to the adult table."
Trump plans to discuss Iran in the trilateral meeting but not Ukraine, the official said, because China is not part of the separate US-Russia track.
